name: Sulfur (topical)

lead: Topical sulfur is a long-established ingredient in acne washes, masks and spot treatments, and is also used for rosacea, seborrhoeic dermatitis and scabies.

Dermatology reviews list sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide among rosacea therapies backed by multiple randomised trials. For acne specifically, the available sources include a label and a comedogenicity study but few controlled efficacy trials.

paras: Sulfur is generally described as keratolytic and antimicrobial, though the reviewed sources give little mechanistic detail.

OTC acne products carry external-use-only warnings. A randomised study found no link between sulfur and comedone formation under its conditions. Trials in scabies and hand eczema did not highlight prominent adverse effects in their abstracts.

lead: Topical sulfur is one of the oldest dermatological treatments, used in lotions, creams, soaps, masks and spot treatments for acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea and scabies. It is sold over the counter in the United States in products labelled for acne.[1]

For appearance purposes it is used mainly for acne. Dermatology reviews describe topical sulfur combined with sodium sulfacetamide as one of the rosacea therapies validated by more than one randomised controlled trial, and randomised trials have also tested sulfur in scabies and hand eczema.[2][3][4][5] Trial evidence for sulfur as a standalone acne treatment is thinner in the sources reviewed, and registered acne studies involving sulfur combinations are of unknown status.[6]
infobox: OTC in the US for acne (labelled products)[1]

paras: A US over-the-counter spot treatment label lists sulfur for the treatment of acne and carries a for-external-use-only warning.[1] A 1978 randomised study that re-examined whether sulfur is comedogenic, in two institutions with groups of 12 and 40 subjects, found no trend linking sulfur in the test formulation to comedone formation; the vehicle used in the study appeared comedogenic.[7] Registered trials of sulfur combinations in acne include a phase 4 study with benzoyl peroxide; its status is listed as unknown.[6]

Two 2005 reviews in Cutis listed topical sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide, alongside topical metronidazole, topical azelaic acid and oral tetracyclines, among rosacea therapies supported by more than one randomised controlled trial.[2][3] A 2023 real-world analysis in Japanese patients compared sulfur and metronidazole preparations for rosacea.[8]

Topical sulfur ointments are used against scabies. The Japanese Dermatological Association guideline notes sulfur preparations are the only topical scabies drugs covered by national health insurance there but describes their usefulness as limited, and reviews of scabies in resource-limited settings list sulfur alongside ivermectin and benzyl benzoate.[9][10] A randomised comparison in 97 Iraqi patients tested 8 and 10 percent sulfur ointment under different application schedules.[4] In a 2024 triple-blind trial in 70 patients with hand eczema, 2 percent sulfur cream and 0.1 percent triamcinolone cream both reduced severity scores over four weeks.[5]

Sulfur is commonly described as having keratolytic and antimicrobial properties. The sources reviewed do not set out its mechanism in detail, and its action in acne and rosacea has not been explained in the trial literature summarised here.

Over-the-counter labels advise external use only.[1] The comedogenicity study found no association between sulfur and comedone formation in its test conditions.[7] A scabies trial and a hand eczema trial of sulfur reported efficacy outcomes without prominent adverse effects in the abstracts available.[5][4]

Randomised evidence includes: sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide for rosacea, summarised in two reviews;[2][3] a comedogenicity study in 52 subjects across two institutions;[7] an RCT in scabies (97 patients) comparing application regimens of 8 and 10 percent sulfur ointment;[4] and a 70-patient RCT in hand eczema finding 2 percent sulfur cream comparable to 0.1 percent triamcinolone over four weeks, with benefits lasting through follow-up.[5] A registered acne trial combining sulfur with benzoyl peroxide has unknown status.[6]
